title: Broker VIP Programmes: Why a Tier Is Not a Service Strategy
summary: An account balance can tell a broker that a client qualifies for VIP treatment. It cannot tell the broker what would make that treatment valuable. Two clients may qualify for the same tier and have very little in common when they ask for help. Spreads, fees and account tiers sit close to the trade. ...
content:
An account balance can tell a broker that a client qualifies for VIP treatment. It cannot tell the broker what would make that treatment valuable. Two clients may qualify for the same tier and have very little in common when they ask for help. Spreads, fees and account tiers sit close to the trade. The client's life does not.

VIP programme design gets this wrong more often than it should. Eligibility is an institutional decision. Relevance is a personal one. Giving everyone in a tier access to the same service makes sense; assuming that everyone wants the same things does not.

The difference matters commercially. A financial firm can spend money making a benefit more impressive without making it more useful. In a broker VIP programme, the service is retention infrastructure, not a perks catalogue, and it only does that job if the clients in the tier actually use it. Before adding another privilege to the list, ask whether the programme is flexible enough to serve the people already entitled to it.

Eligibility answers only the first question

Clear tiers have a purpose. They define access, establish expectations and help a firm decide what it can afford to provide. I am not arguing for abandoning them. I am arguing against treating a qualification rule as a complete description of a customer.

The missing information is often ordinary: how the client travels, which arrangements they prefer to delegate, whether family needs are relevant, and how much involvement they want in a decision. That information should come from a conversation about the service. A financial account should not be treated as permission to infer or collect every detail of someone's private life.

Two requests, different priorities

Two real cases from Perfect.Live's operational records show how different the work behind a request can be.

In one, a member was away on a business trip when his car on Madeira was due for scheduled maintenance. We arranged the ferry crossing and towing, delivered the car to an authorised service centre in Lisbon, oversaw the work and had it back at his villa before he arrived.

This was routine work made complicated by distance: a chain of providers the member never had to manage himself.

In another, ahead of an official wedding ceremony in Monaco, a member found she lacked the original certified copy of her birth certificate. We organised an emergency retrieval from a London archive, and a personal courier placed the document in her hands in less than 24 hours.

Here nothing could be rescheduled. When a document is missing and the date is fixed, the client needs someone who owns the problem until it is solved, not a list of benefits.

Neither request had anything to do with trading. Both are the kind of help a broker's top clients need and no account tier provides. A programme needs room for routine coordination and for urgent, time-sensitive help; a list of prestige benefits covers neither.

Standardise responsibility, personalise the work

Personalisation does not require a different operating model for every customer. Some things should be consistent: an understandable route to assistance, clear approval of spending, realistic commitments and someone responsible for taking the request through to completion.

What changes is the work within that structure. One client wants options before making each choice. Another wants the team to organise arrangements within agreed instructions and return only when a decision is needed. Both can receive the same standard of service without being forced through an identical interaction.

At Perfect.Live, a global concierge and lifestyle management ecosystem, we distinguish between tailoring the programme to the business and tailoring the service to each customer. The institution's proposition, delivered under its own brand, sets the framework. A client's actual request gives the lifestyle manager the context to act within it.

Our technology, built in-house, gives the client one place to ask and the institution oversight of the programme. Perfect.Live reports that 98% of clients receive a first response within two minutes, and a named lifestyle manager then owns each request from the first message to completion. That combination is what lets one standard of service respond to very different needs.

Relevant does not mean unlimited

There is a commercial discipline to this. A broad promise of personal assistance is not permission to promise anything to anyone. The programme needs to say what access includes, which requests it can handle and which purchases the client pays for separately.

Access to help arranging a flight is different from a flight paid for by the broker. The same distinction applies to hotels, tickets and experiences. If those boundaries are vague, the client and the institution may have very different ideas about the benefit being offered.

A provider also should not have to invent an exceptional experience to justify every interaction. A routine arrangement completed reliably is often the right service, and forcing glamour into the proposition distracts from the less visible work clients actually want to delegate.

Give VIP clients a reason to use private concierge and lifestyle management

A benefits page describes availability, not relevance. A client may know that concierge is included and still assume it is only for expensive restaurants or special access, rather than a personal assistant for the practical side of their life. If the same programme solves a travel problem on a Tuesday and a family logistics problem on a Sunday, the broker becomes part of the client's operating life rather than one of several trading accounts.

Make the introduction practical: explain the types of arrangements the team handles, the boundaries of the service, and how to make a first request. Let the account manager raise the service when it is relevant, not only at onboarding. Then let the client decide when it is useful. That says more than another assertion that the programme is exclusive.

Feedback should go beyond whether a request was completed. Was this the help the client expected? What did they want to delegate that the service could not handle? Repeated answers show where the proposition needs to change, including where a benefit is a poor fit.

The first test is whether people recognise a use for the benefit and receive the help they expected. A programme that improves on those answers will do more for the relationship than one that adds privileges to make the list longer.

A VIP tier should define the commitment a firm makes; the service gives that commitment meaning for each client. The title on the account may be the same. What makes it worth having should be allowed to differ.

About the author

Dmitri Laush is CEO and Co-Founder of Perfect.Live, a global concierge and lifestyle management ecosystem for high-net-worth individuals and the businesses that serve them. Operating since 2017, Perfect.Live works 24/7 across 127 countries and delivers its human-led service to brokers, exchanges, fintechs and private banks under the partner's own brand, on a platform it builds in-house.

An account balance can tell a broker that a client qualifies for VIP treatment. It cannot tell the broker what would make that treatment valuable. Two clients may qualify for the same tier and have very little in common when they ask for help. Spreads, fees and account tiers sit close to the trade. The client's life does not.

VIP programme design gets this wrong more often than it should. Eligibility is an institutional decision. Relevance is a personal one. Giving everyone in a tier access to the same service makes sense; assuming that everyone wants the same things does not.

The difference matters commercially. A financial firm can spend money making a benefit more impressive without making it more useful. In a broker VIP programme, the service is retention infrastructure, not a perks catalogue, and it only does that job if the clients in the tier actually use it. Before adding another privilege to the list, ask whether the programme is flexible enough to serve the people already entitled to it.

Eligibility answers only the first question

Clear tiers have a purpose. They define access, establish expectations and help a firm decide what it can afford to provide. I am not arguing for abandoning them. I am arguing against treating a qualification rule as a complete description of a customer.

The missing information is often ordinary: how the client travels, which arrangements they prefer to delegate, whether family needs are relevant, and how much involvement they want in a decision. That information should come from a conversation about the service. A financial account should not be treated as permission to infer or collect every detail of someone's private life.

Two requests, different priorities

Two real cases from Perfect.Live's operational records show how different the work behind a request can be.

In one, a member was away on a business trip when his car on Madeira was due for scheduled maintenance. We arranged the ferry crossing and towing, delivered the car to an authorised service centre in Lisbon, oversaw the work and had it back at his villa before he arrived.

This was routine work made complicated by distance: a chain of providers the member never had to manage himself.

In another, ahead of an official wedding ceremony in Monaco, a member found she lacked the original certified copy of her birth certificate. We organised an emergency retrieval from a London archive, and a personal courier placed the document in her hands in less than 24 hours.

Here nothing could be rescheduled. When a document is missing and the date is fixed, the client needs someone who owns the problem until it is solved, not a list of benefits.

Neither request had anything to do with trading. Both are the kind of help a broker's top clients need and no account tier provides. A programme needs room for routine coordination and for urgent, time-sensitive help; a list of prestige benefits covers neither.

Standardise responsibility, personalise the work

Personalisation does not require a different operating model for every customer. Some things should be consistent: an understandable route to assistance, clear approval of spending, realistic commitments and someone responsible for taking the request through to completion.

What changes is the work within that structure. One client wants options before making each choice. Another wants the team to organise arrangements within agreed instructions and return only when a decision is needed. Both can receive the same standard of service without being forced through an identical interaction.

At Perfect.Live, a global concierge and lifestyle management ecosystem, we distinguish between tailoring the programme to the business and tailoring the service to each customer. The institution's proposition, delivered under its own brand, sets the framework. A client's actual request gives the lifestyle manager the context to act within it.

Our technology, built in-house, gives the client one place to ask and the institution oversight of the programme. Perfect.Live reports that 98% of clients receive a first response within two minutes, and a named lifestyle manager then owns each request from the first message to completion. That combination is what lets one standard of service respond to very different needs.

Relevant does not mean unlimited

There is a commercial discipline to this. A broad promise of personal assistance is not permission to promise anything to anyone. The programme needs to say what access includes, which requests it can handle and which purchases the client pays for separately.

Access to help arranging a flight is different from a flight paid for by the broker. The same distinction applies to hotels, tickets and experiences. If those boundaries are vague, the client and the institution may have very different ideas about the benefit being offered.

A provider also should not have to invent an exceptional experience to justify every interaction. A routine arrangement completed reliably is often the right service, and forcing glamour into the proposition distracts from the less visible work clients actually want to delegate.

Give VIP clients a reason to use private concierge and lifestyle management

A benefits page describes availability, not relevance. A client may know that concierge is included and still assume it is only for expensive restaurants or special access, rather than a personal assistant for the practical side of their life. If the same programme solves a travel problem on a Tuesday and a family logistics problem on a Sunday, the broker becomes part of the client's operating life rather than one of several trading accounts.

Make the introduction practical: explain the types of arrangements the team handles, the boundaries of the service, and how to make a first request. Let the account manager raise the service when it is relevant, not only at onboarding. Then let the client decide when it is useful. That says more than another assertion that the programme is exclusive.

Feedback should go beyond whether a request was completed. Was this the help the client expected? What did they want to delegate that the service could not handle? Repeated answers show where the proposition needs to change, including where a benefit is a poor fit.

The first test is whether people recognise a use for the benefit and receive the help they expected. A programme that improves on those answers will do more for the relationship than one that adds privileges to make the list longer.

A VIP tier should define the commitment a firm makes; the service gives that commitment meaning for each client. The title on the account may be the same. What makes it worth having should be allowed to differ.

summary:

Tuesday, 24/11/2026 | 11:00 GMT by Damian Chmiel

  • The paid connection lets brokers using both firms send trading and pricing data outside the public internet.
  • Brokers pay setup and recurring fees to each firm, while a June deal had a liquidity provider covering the tools.

Your Bourse and NetShop ISP have opened a private fiber connection between their servers in two Equinix data centers near London, the companies said today (Tuesday). Brokers that use both the trading technology provider and the hosting company can ask for it to be switched on.

The cross-connect joins NetShop's equipment at Equinix LD4 with Your Bourse's trading systems at LD6, two buildings on the same Slough campus. Trading and pricing data between them no longer cross the public internet. Each firm charges separately for setup and upkeep.

Your Bourse told FinanceMagnates.com it has not run comparative latency or jitter tests on the link. It said clients who moved to it no longer had the latency and jitter problems they had before.

London's trading industry is coming home!

Built After Requests From Shared Clients

The companies said the connection followed requests from brokers that host servers with NetShop and route execution through Your Bourse.

"When execution consistency matters, every hop you remove counts," said Stefano Sordini, chief executive of NetShop ISP.

Sordini said having the link already in place takes the setup work off brokers that use both companies.

NetShop, based in Cyprus, sells hosting , colocation and managed services to FX brokers, prop trading firms and technology vendors. Retail FX brokers are also the market FM Intelligence's broker volumes tracker follows quarter by quarter.

The Slough campus has drawn that business for years. oneZero cited the large dealers keeping servers there when it moved its systems into LD4 in 2014 to cut latency for clients.

Who Pays for the Technology

Two earlier Your Bourse tie-ups this year answered differently the question of who carries the cost of the broker's technology.

In June, Your Bourse added Advanced Markets to its premium liquidity provider roster. The liquidity provider sponsored the bridge, matching engine and reporting tools, so brokers paid no separate fee for them.

The tie-up with Dubai-focused 4XPORTAL in October came without a joint package, and Your Bourse said two to three brokers used the combined setup at the time.

Brokers taking the NetShop link pay both providers. Each firm offers preferential terms to eligible clients the other refers.

Across the three, only the June deal took the technology bill off the broker.

title: FM Summit London 2026 Live from Old Billingsgate: Manipulation Risks Meet Consumer Duty in Prediction Markets Debate
summary:
The 15th edition of the Finance Magnates London Summit (FMLS) is officially underway today, November 24, 2026, returning to its historic riverside venue at Old Billingsgate, London. 
After last night’s Opening Networking Blitz at The Folly, the summit packs executive keynotes, invite-only roundtable...
content:
The 15th edition of the Finance Magnates London Summit (FMLS) is officially underway today, November 24, 2026, returning to its historic riverside venue at Old Billingsgate, London.

After last night’s Opening Networking Blitz at The Folly, the summit packs executive keynotes, invite-only roundtables, and B2B networking into one high-density day.

Follow our live coverage below for real-time insights.

AI & Trading 2027: From Copilots to Colleagues

The agenda kicked off with a discussion surrounding AI. With frontier models now widely accessible to any firm, competitive advantage in the trading industry has shifted toward proprietary data quality and runtime governance.

Moderated by ForexBrokers.com Global Director of Research Steven J. Hatzakis, infrastructure builders and brokerage executives, including Yangling Li (BestX), Andrew Ralich (oneZero), Jon Light (Devexperts), Hugh Whelan (ACI UK, Financial Markets Association), and Christoforos Theodoulou (MetaQuotes), compare what has genuinely reached production versus what still lacks the traceability and regulatory guardrails required to trust autonomous agents on a live desk.

Responding to an audience question about the surge of "vibe coding" and DIY AI trading tools lowering entry barriers for retail participants, oneZero CEO and Co-Founder Andrew Ralich noted that his firm has intentionally held off on launching end-trader agentic tools while it focuses on auditability, guardrails, and predictability for broker clients.

Ralich cautioned that expanding direct API access without strict oversight risks stripping away protections that previously shielded individual traders.

"My major concern is how much you equip hobbyist retail speculative traders with API capabilities," he said. "You used to have to be a qualified intermediary just to get an API from a broker. I think a lot of protection comes from that for individual clients. And we need to make sure that as we build these solutions out, we're keeping the brokers, the client, everybody accountable for what's actually happening in the system."

The Future of Prop Trading

Roughly a third of prop trading firms have vanished over the past two years, leaving a $20 billion sector where payout rates hover near 7% and discount wars continue to squeeze margins.

Finance Magnates Editor-in-Chief Yam Yehoshua spoke with Drew Niv (ATFX), Felix Strasser (CMC Markets), and Elina Pedersen (Your Bourse) examining how challenge-model economics, A-book/B-book risk strategies, and hybrid broker-prop partnerships are reshaping the sector’s path into regulated trading.

Lord Peter Cruddas in Conversation

CMC Markets Founder and CEO Lord Peter Cruddas sat down with Finance Magnates’ Jonathan Fine to trace an unconventional forty-year journey, from working as a weekend milkman at 14 to building a global, billion-dollar neo-investment bank.

Recalling his earliest realisation of the internet’s potential to cut out middlemen and drive down costs — joking that he initially wondered if he could buy "this company called the internet" — Cruddas explained how launching online trading in October and pioneering CFDs dismantled the barriers of the "black-and-white days," when investors needed separate futures, stockbroking, and FX accounts to access different asset classes.

By consolidating global products into a single account and driving down costs for everyday "mom and dad" investors, he noted, the industry fundamentally democratized market access.

"It’s now possible for a taxi driver to pull over to the side of the road, trade 10,000 or 20,000 of the world’s products in real time, and get the same execution prices as Goldman Sachs. That’s what we have done for this industry; we’ve opened up the world’s financial markets so that ordinary people, everybody, can participate," he said.

Addressing the future of digital assets, Lord Peter Cruddas drew a firm line between speculative tokens and blockchain settlement rails, rejecting popular anti-inflationary narratives around standalone cryptocurrencies while predicting that stablecoins and multi-asset wallets will allow millions of global investors to trade directly with one another and bypass traditional exchanges within the next decade:

"I think cryptocurrencies as a standalone product are pure speculation. I know there's debates around 'they're anti-inflationary, governments printing money' — I don't buy into any of that. But I am a big believer in cryptocurrency as a stablecoin to change the way people trade in the future. In the next 10 years, I think we'll all be trading with each other directly using a multi-asset wallet, using a stablecoin to buy and sell from each other."

Looking Ahead to 2027: Where Brokers Are Actually Finding Growth

With client acquisition costs climbing, traditional regions saturated, and product lineups looking increasingly uniform across brokerages, executives were trying to identify what is genuinely moving the needle ahead of 2027.

Moderated by LiquidityFinder Founder Sam Low, panelists Alex Piliavsky (Alchemy Avenue), John Kinghorn (Peratera), Christiana Vasiadou (Global Markets Group Limited), Chariton Christou (Boltzmann Research), and Marios Chailis (Libertex Group) separated high-traction products and automation wins from industry hype.

Libertex Group CMO Marios Chailis argued that speed of adoption will separate winners from laggards, warning that "the only brokers that are going to have a problem with AI are the brokers that do not adopt it fast enough and introduce it as part of their risk management and client experience."

On the client side, retail traders are increasingly deploying AI bots and Model Context Protocol (MCP) connections to automate their strategies. Against this background, the panel warned that brokerages face growing pressure to upgrade their risk controls and internal infrastructure.

Meanwhile, Global Markets Group Limited CEO and Compliance Officer Christiana Vasiadou highlighted the regulatory questions emerging around trade ownership and client protection when retail traders hand execution over to generic AI agents.

"The question is — and this is something that the FCA is looking into — who is actually trading? Who owns the trade: is it the agent or the client?" she asked. "At the end of the day, the broker has to accept this business is getting more and more common, and providing the right controls in this environment maybe can be a sub-account, so that if the AI agent goes rogue, it doesn't deplete the account completely; also providing a kill switch in case something goes wrong."

Does Your LinkedIn Feed Need More AI Writing?

Stepping away from market mechanics, this afternoon debate tackled the explosion of AI-generated thought-leadership content across financial services LinkedIn feeds.

Moderated by Started PR Founder Kimberley Waldron, Finance Magnates’ Jonathan Fine and City A.M.’s Anna Moloney discussed whether generative AI democratizes industry insights and elevates communication, or simply erodes reader trust with generic corporate filler – or as the zeitgeist has termed it, ‘AI slop.’

Arguing in favor of AI-assisted writing, Fine compared contemporary fears over 'AI slop' to Plato’s 370 BC critique warning that the invention of writing would breed superficial knowledge and erode human memory. Just as society adapted to earlier communication tools, Fine argued that resisting generative AI on professional feeds is a battle already lost.

"While we've seen a decent amount of quill slop and pen slop since, we embraced the technology and we're quite fine with it. Here too, I would like to argue that AI is not the problem; the battle against the problem is already decided, and if anything, AI can be part of the solution," he said.

Young Fintech Talent Pitches to Trading Veterans

Four early-stage fintech teams, all alumni of Work in Fintech hackathons, took the stage for five-minute pitches and live product demos.

Moderated by ipushpull CEO Matthew Cheung, a judging panel featuring Chris Knight (LMAX Digital), Mehul Patel (Newsquawk), Stephen Totten (OneZero), Laurence Booth (CMC Markets), and Paul Humphrey (BMLL) evaluated how close these emerging concepts are to solving real problems on institutional trading desks.

The founding team behind Moneywell Town, startup Vasmio, won first place. It showcased a retro, browser-based RPG aimed at closing the financial literacy gap among UK 15-to-18-year-olds.

Designed around the concept "Learn money in town. Get quizzed in the outskirts," the game teaches teens the fundamentals of tax, credit, saving, interest, mortgages, and scams before testing their retention through creature battles.

Fresh off winning first place out of 20 teams at the Work in Fintech AI Hackathon in August 2026, the founders pitched a B2B2C model using schools for distribution while partnering with banks and building societies to fund impartial education pilots.

Should Prediction Markets Be Banned for Retail Investors?

Closing out the forum, the discussion circled back to prediction markets. This head-on clash confronted the rapid rise of retail event contracts, and whether they amount to repackaged binary options.

Moderated by Finance Magnates’ Jonathan Fine, Interactive Brokers UK CEO Gerald Perez and Blackheath Advisors CEO Laura McCracken debate whether prediction markets represent a legitimate mechanism for risk transfer or speculative gambling that regulators should bar from retail access.

McCracken recounted how she was initially captivated by prediction markets during the US elections after watching them outperform traditional pollsters. However, she argued that the sector has since been undermined by unintended consequences, chief among them market manipulation and insider trading.

Pointing to how wealthy actors can drop millions into thinly traded contracts not to win a payout, but to manufacture momentum and shift public perception, McCracken warned that the platforms are easily weaponized.

"Whenever you have this kind of market, you have players that come in and they take this truth and they turn it into an opportunity to manipulate, turning it into a PR machine," she said, adding that, "Do you not think that they're going to put money into the betting markets to sway a school of thought? Absolutely they are."

Arguing against the motion to bar retail investors from prediction markets, Interactive Brokers UK CEO Gerald Perez rejected a blanket ban, noting that event contracts span legitimate economic and climate risks that everyday investors use to hedge exposure.

Challenging the industry's commitment to market democratization if retail traders are locked out, Perez argued that UK regulators already have the framework to oversee the product safely.

"How can we speak democratization when we exclude the little guy?" he said, adding that, "We all know about the Consumer Duty in this country. Are you telling me we can't put guardrails? We've done it with options, we've done it with crypto, we've done it with FX."

"How can we speak democratization when we exclude the little guy?" he said, adding that, "We all know about the Consumer Duty in this country. Are you telling me we can't put guardrails? We've done it with options, we've done it with crypto, we've done it with FX."

title: Could Bitcoin’s Price Decline Increase Demand for Stablecoins?
summary:
One of the most attractive aspects of cryptocurrency investments has always been associated with the relative liquidity of this marketplace. However, this silver lining can often be obscured by a
The post Could Bitcoin’s Price Decline Increase Demand for Stablecoins?  appeared first on CryptoNinjas.
content:
One of the most attractive aspects of cryptocurrency investments has always been associated with the relative liquidity of this marketplace. However, this silver lining can often be obscured by a cloud of volatility. The fact that Bitcoin has tested its lowest levels since April 2026 clearly signals that a readjustment may be in order. Investors are also worried, as the recent dip below $74,000 might indicate that another round of bearish sentiment is soon to take hold.

Should traders liquidate their current positions? Might it be better to short all cryptocurrencies for the moment? Although there can be arguments made for both of these strategies, we need to remember that hedging is still a very real possibility. Stablecoins pegged to the United States dollar could represent the safest port in this storm, and it pays to take a closer look at why some astute traders are adopting this rather conservative mindset. 

  • How Dollar-Pegged Stablecoins Maintain Their Value 
  • Why Stablecoin Demand May Change During Market Volatility 
  • Stablecoin Use Cases Beyond Cryptocurrency Trading 
  • Risks and Limitations of Stablecoins
  • Conclusion: What Bitcoin Volatility Could Mean for Stablecoin Demand 

How Dollar-Pegged Stablecoins Maintain Their Value 

As the name already suggests, stablecoins are often capable of superseding (at least to an extent) some of the volatility that can be attributed to open-market crypto volatility. This arises from how they function. Unlike other tokens, stablecoins are directly pegged to the dollar at roughly $1 per coin. Note that they may also be linked to other US assets, such as short-term treasuries. So what happens if the price begins to dip?

Assuming that the value of a stablecoin, such as USDC, dramatically falls below its $1 value, arbitrageurs will often choose to purchase these tokens at a lower value. This serves two primary purposes:

  • It enables them to become involved on a dip (securing potentially higher profit margins)
  • Large-scale purchases help to boost prices back to a relative 1:1 parity. 

However, there is another reason why stablecoins represent attractive assets during times of uncertainty. 

Why Stablecoin Demand May Change During Market Volatility 

One of the misconceptions that has been attributed to cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin is the belief that the sheer value of this asset makes it somewhat immune to short-term price swings. The recent performance of Bitcoin should clearly illustrate otherwise. The fact of the matter is that the vast majority of crypto tokens, and meme coins, are affected by several variables. These include market sentiment, supply, demand, speculation, and sudden cascading liquidations.

Stablecoins function in a slightly different manner. Thanks to their inherent relationship with the dollar, they can be used as a more “stable” medium of exchange when other tokens may begin to exhibit pear-shaped movements. 

Stablecoin Use Cases Beyond Cryptocurrency Trading 

Another potent argument which stablecoin pundits will often make involves the utilitarian nature of these tokens. For instance, some readers may not be aware that they can often serve as a substitute for fiat when playing online blockchain-based games may offer. Well-known examples include Tether and USD Coin; two options that a growing number of iGaming providers work with.

This is pivotal when it comes to real-world applications. Unlike meme coins, and even a handful of major cryptocurrencies, the fact that stablecoins can now double as viable transfer options has helped to increase demand, and if chart values fall, they are not likely to suffer from a lack of liquidity. 

Risks and Limitations of Stablecoins

Any article discussing the merits of specific cryptocurrencies must seek to adopt a fair, and balanced approach. This is why it is just as logical to highlight some pitfalls that could impact a stablecoin investment. 

Perhaps the most obvious concern involves what would happen if a stablecoin were suddenly de-pegged from its underlying currency. While this is unlikely, another problem has already been illustrated in the past. Some readers may recall the devaluation of USDC once it was discovered that this stablecoin was linked to the failing Silicon Valley Bank. Confidence essentially collapsed, and the value of USDC plummeted. 

A final stumbling block is directly tied to inflation. Cryptocurrencies have been traditionally associated with hedges against inflationary rates. This is not the case with stablecoins due to their relationship with fiat. In other words, the value of tokens can be directly impacted by rising, or falling, inflationary data. If interest rates begin to rise, borrowing costs will follow suit. This makes it more expensive to purchase crypto, and investors are more likely to turn to low-risk positions (such as high-yield savings accounts). 

Conclusion: What Bitcoin Volatility Could Mean for Stablecoin Demand 

We can now see why some astute traders have been turning to stablecoins as a means to offset recent market jitters. However, this does not signify that such assets represent a win-win situation. Risks should always be balanced with potential rewards, and investors should allocate more funds than they are prepared to lose. 

Might Bitcoin continue to fall? Will we soon reach a stable level of support before the end of 2026? This question is on everyone’s mind, and time will tell.

title: Binance Hack: US Moves to Recover $1.1 Billion, but Who Gets the Money?
summary: Key takeaways US authorities filed a civil forfeiture complaint on November 23 seeking more than $1.1 billion in USDC linked to the October 29 Binance hack, across 36 addresses on 18 blockchains. Circle froze the funds but says it cannot technically move them, so it proposes issuing replacement USDC...
content:
Key takeaways

  • US authorities filed a civil forfeiture complaint on November 23 seeking more than $1.1 billion in USDC linked to the October 29 Binance hack, across 36 addresses on 18 blockchains.
  • Circle froze the funds but says it cannot technically move them, so it proposes issuing replacement USDC to the US after a forfeiture order.
  • Frozen is not recovered: the filings advance the legal-control stage, while final distribution and ownership remain undecided.
  • A separate Abu Dhabi court order adds a second jurisdiction, and Circle’s reserve and supply reporting for the replacement tokens will deserve scrutiny.

Nearly four weeks after the Binance hack, US authorities have filed a civil forfeiture complaint seeking more than $1.1 billion in USDC linked to the October theft. The money is already subject to restrictions, but the latest court filings reveal a complication: freezing stolen cryptocurrency is considerably easier than returning it.

The complaint, filed on November 23, in the US District Court for the District of Columbia, targets USDC associated with 36 cryptocurrency addresses across 18 blockchains.

Federal investigators attribute the October 29 attack to North Korean hacking groups, including the Lazarus Group. The complaint puts the value of the original theft at approximately $6 billion.

For Binance, the latest legal action represents another opportunity to recover a portion of its losses. For the wider cryptocurrency industry, however, the case raises questions about the authority stablecoin issuers exercise over digital assets and what happens when governments become involved.

Binance Hack Recovery Enters a New Legal Phase

The assets targeted by US authorities are not an entirely new discovery.

Earlier this month, NewsBTC reported that Circle had frozen approximately $1.1 billion in USDC linked to the Binance hack, following cooperation with law enforcement.

What has changed is the government’s attempt to establish a legal basis for taking possession of those assets.

According to the court documents, US authorities obtained a temporary restraining order on November 12. Prosecutors subsequently requested that the restrictions remain in place throughout the civil forfeiture proceedings.

Both Binance and Circle consented to the initial restraining order and the requested extension, according to the government’s November 23 application.

The agreement between the companies and federal authorities reduces one immediate obstacle to preserving the funds. It does not, however, resolve the question of their ultimate ownership or distribution.

Civil forfeiture proceedings are directed against property believed to be connected to criminal activity. Interested parties can assert legitimate claims to that property through the legal process.

In this case, prosecutors are seeking forfeiture of the assets to the United States. That is not the same thing as a court ordering their immediate return to Binance.

Circle Cannot Simply Send the Frozen USDC Back

Perhaps the most interesting disclosure in the complaint concerns Circle itself.

The stablecoin issuer can restrict transfers involving USDC held at particular blockchain addresses. However, that authority does not necessarily give Circle direct control over the wallets holding those tokens.

The complaint states that Circle:

“

does not have the technical ability to transfer the Defendant Property from the blocklisted Subject Addresses to the United States

Instead, Circle has agreed to issue an equivalent amount of replacement USDC and transfer those tokens to US authorities upon receiving a forfeiture order from the court.

The proposed arrangement exposes an unusual feature of centralized stablecoins. An issuer can prevent tokens from circulating without possessing the private keys needed to move them.

It also raises an accounting question that deserves attention. If replacement tokens are issued, what ultimately happens to the original frozen USDC, and how will Circle ensure that the treatment of those balances is reflected accurately in its outstanding supply and reserve reporting?

The issuance of replacement tokens would not, by itself, prove that USDC had become undercollateralized. Nevertheless, transparency around the implementation would be important for a stablecoin whose credibility depends on confidence in its backing.

The immediate concern is not whether Circle can create new tokens. It is whether the entire recovery process can be independently accounted for.

The $1.1 Billion Is Not Back With Binance Yet

The temptation to describe the Justice Department’s announcement as a billion-dollar recovery is understandable. It is also premature.

There are three separate stages involved: restricting access to the stolen assets, obtaining legal authority over them and determining how they will ultimately be distributed.

The November 23 filings advance the second stage. They do not establish that the third has been completed.

The $1.1 billion Binance recovery process. Source: US District Court for the District of Columbia filings, November 23, 2026.

There is also a cross-border complication.

On November 18, Reuters reported that an Abu Dhabi court had directed several cryptocurrency companies, including Circle, to preserve digital assets associated with the Binance theft.

The involvement of authorities in both the United States and the United Arab Emirates illustrates how a single cryptocurrency theft can generate legal proceedings across multiple jurisdictions.

Blockchain transactions may cross national borders without much difficulty. Establishing ownership rights over the assets involved is a considerably less straightforward exercise.

That does not mean the US and UAE proceedings are necessarily in conflict. But the ultimate disposition of the funds will require more than an announcement from either government.

For investors assessing Binance’s financial position, the distinction between frozen assets and recovered capital is particularly important. Restricted cryptocurrency should not automatically be treated as money already returned to the exchange.

The Binance Hack Tests the Case for Centralized Stablecoins

For years, the ability of stablecoin issuers to freeze tokens has been criticized by advocates of decentralized finance.

The Binance case demonstrates the other side of that argument.

Without Circle’s ability to restrict transactions, preserving such a large amount of cryptocurrency for potential recovery would have been more difficult.

In this particular case, centralized control has provided a mechanism that may help prevent suspected criminals from benefiting from stolen assets.

The uncomfortable question is whether the cryptocurrency industry can benefit from that authority while also demanding meaningful safeguards against its misuse.

The answer depends partly on transparency. Token holders should be able to understand why assets were frozen, under what legal authority restrictions remain in place and how disputes over ownership are resolved.

The same standard should apply to the exchange, the stablecoin issuer and the government.

The next significant development in the Binance case will be the court’s treatment of the forfeiture claim and any competing claims to the assets. Circle’s proposed issuance of replacement USDC will also deserve scrutiny if it proceeds.

Until then, the $1.1 billion should be understood as assets subject to an ongoing recovery effort, not a completed repayment.

For a cryptocurrency industry that frequently celebrates the speed of moving money, the Binance hack is a reminder that getting it back can be an entirely different business.

title: Bitcoin Reserves Just Found a New Use on Wall Street, but There’s a Catch
summary: Key takeaways CFTC staff guidance issued on November 23 says swap execution facilities, designated contract markets and clearinghouses may count Bitcoin, Ether and qualifying payment stablecoins toward certain financial resource requirements. The advisory references a minimum 20% haircut for Bitcoin...
content:
Key takeaways

  • CFTC staff guidance issued on November 23 says swap execution facilities, designated contract markets and clearinghouses may count Bitcoin, Ether and qualifying payment stablecoins toward certain financial resource requirements.
  • The advisory references a minimum 20% haircut for Bitcoin and Ethereum, so a $10 million Bitcoin reserve would count as $8 million, and 2% for qualifying payment stablecoins.
  • Crypto cannot be used to meet the separate cash and liquid-resources requirement, which covers three months for swap execution facilities and generally six months for the other two types of venue.
  • It is a staff advisory, not a binding rule, and nothing in it requires institutions to buy Bitcoin.

Bitcoin reserves have found another potential use within the US financial system. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has clarified that regulated derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses can count Bitcoin, Ethereum and qualifying payment stablecoins toward certain financial resource requirements. However, the regulator is not prepared to treat those holdings like cash.

The guidance, issued on November 23, could give regulated trading venues greater flexibility in managing their balance sheets. For Bitcoin investors, however, the more interesting question is whether that flexibility will translate into fresh institutional demand.

The answer is not quite as straightforward as it might seem.

CFTC Gives Bitcoin Reserves a New Role in Financial Markets

The CFTC’s latest advisory addresses three types of regulated businesses: swap execution facilities, designated contract markets and derivatives clearing organizations.

These institutions are required to maintain sufficient financial resources to cover at least one year of operating costs. Under the new staff guidance, Bitcoin, Ether and qualifying payment stablecoins may contribute toward those requirements, subject to appropriate valuation discounts.

The announcement follows broader efforts to integrate digital assets into regulated financial infrastructure. NewsBTC previously reported on the CFTC’s guidance concerning tokenized collateral at clearinghouses, another area where traditional financial markets are gradually accommodating blockchain-based assets.

This time, the discussion is not about what traders can post as collateral. It is about the assets that the institutions running those markets can rely on to keep their businesses operating.

For a company that already holds Bitcoin, the clarification could make those holdings more useful from a regulatory standpoint. For businesses considering adding cryptocurrency to their balance sheets, it removes some uncertainty surrounding how those assets would be recognized.

But that recognition comes at a discount!

A $10 Million Bitcoin Reserve Is Worth $8 Million on Paper

The CFTC advisory references a minimum 20% valuation haircut for Bitcoin and Ethereum, consistent with earlier staff treatment of proprietary cryptocurrency positions held by futures commission merchants.

Qualifying payment stablecoins receive considerably more favorable treatment, with a referenced haircut of 2%.

An exchange holding $10 million in Bitcoin, for example, would be able to count $8 million toward the relevant financial resource requirement if it applied a 20% haircut and no further deductions were necessary.

The remaining $2 million is not a realized loss. It is a regulatory adjustment intended to account for the risk associated with holding a volatile asset.

Crypto assets that are neither readily marketable nor qualifying payment stablecoins would generally face a 100% haircut, effectively excluding them from the calculation.

Perhaps the most revealing part of the advisory is the regulator’s warning about what it calls wrong-way risk.

The CFTC staff specifically states:

“

A DCM should consider potential wrong-way risk

For a cryptocurrency-focused exchange, that risk is particularly relevant. A prolonged Bitcoin sell-off could put pressure on trading revenues while simultaneously reducing the value of the assets the exchange relies on to support its operations.

The problem is not simply that Bitcoin is volatile. It is that its value could deteriorate at precisely the moment a crypto business finds itself under financial pressure.

A 20% valuation discount provides some protection against that scenario, but it is hardly a guarantee.

The CFTC Is Still Drawing a Line Between Bitcoin and Cash

Despite allowing digital assets to contribute toward broader operating resources, the CFTC has maintained a separate requirement for cash and highly liquid securities.

Bitcoin, Ethereum and even qualifying payment stablecoins cannot be used to satisfy that particular obligation under the advisory.

Swap execution facilities must maintain qualifying liquid resources sufficient to cover at least three months of projected operating expenses or the cost of winding down their operations, whichever is greater.

For designated contract markets and derivatives clearing organizations, the operating-cost liquidity requirement generally covers at least six months.

The distinction matters because an institution can have substantial assets on its balance sheet without necessarily having the cash available to meet immediate obligations.

It is also worth noting that the guidance does not address whether cryptocurrencies can satisfy the separate financial resources that clearinghouses must maintain to cover clearing-member defaults.

In effect, the CFTC is recognizing Bitcoin as an asset that can contribute to an institution’s financial strength without giving it the same regulatory standing as cash.

That is a more cautious approach than some Bitcoin advocates might have hoped for, but arguably a more sustainable one for integrating cryptocurrency into financial infrastructure.

Could the Decision Trigger More Institutional Bitcoin Buying?

The bullish interpretation is relatively simple. If regulated financial institutions can derive greater utility from holding Bitcoin, more of them may eventually consider allocating capital to the cryptocurrency.

There is some merit to that argument.

The expansion of regulated crypto infrastructure has already brought digital assets closer to traditional financial markets. Earlier, NewsBTC reported on Coinbase’s CFTC registration for its USDC-focused derivatives clearinghouse, illustrating how cryptocurrency businesses are increasingly operating within established regulatory frameworks.

The latest advisory gives relevant institutions another reason to evaluate how digital assets fit into their balance sheets.

Still, there is a considerable difference between allowing an institution to hold Bitcoin for regulatory purposes and giving it an economic incentive to buy more.

An exchange that already owns Bitcoin could benefit from the clarification without purchasing a single additional coin. Another might conclude that holding conventional securities remains more efficient, particularly given the valuation discounts and separate liquidity requirements.

Nothing in the advisory requires institutions to acquire Bitcoin, and no purchase commitments were disclosed alongside the announcement.

Investors should therefore resist the temptation to translate this development directly into a bullish price forecast.

The longer-term significance may be greater than the immediate market impact. Every additional recognized use for Bitcoin within regulated financial markets strengthens the case for its utility beyond speculative trading.

However, the November 23 document remains a staff advisory rather than a binding rule adopted by the full Commission. It does not amend existing regulations or create enforceable rights.

The next meaningful development will be evidence that regulated institutions are actually changing their reserve allocations in response.

Until then, Bitcoin has gained another form of regulatory recognition. Whether it gains another source of sustained buying pressure is a different question entirely.

Here is a breakdown of how some of these bots help you earn more without constantly monitoring your trades.

  1. Spot Grid

The Spot grid mode splits your starting funds between the two digital assets of your chosen trading pair, say BTC/USDT. The bot then creates a grid of price points between the upper and lower limits and divides your capital equally between the number of grids used.

The bot automatically buys more of the asset when the price drops to a lower grid level. Then, when the price rises to an upper grid level, the spot grid bot automatically sells some of the assets.

Each time the price reaches the upper grid line, the bot automatically sells a portion of the asset and buys the traded asset when the price reaches the lower grid line. You make money from the difference between the prices at which the bot buys and sells.

  1. Futures Grid

The futures grid aims to make money from price fluctuations within a range. OKX offers various types of futures grid strategies:

  • Long Futures Grid: The bot buys futures at the current price and sells them when the price rises. This strategy is best for markets that are expected to go up but still have some volatility.
  • Short Futures Grid: The bot sells futures at the current price and buys them back when the price drops. This strategy is best for markets that expect to go down but still have some volatility.
  • Neutral Futures Grid: The bot trades in both directions, buying when the price is low and selling when it’s high, no matter the market trend.

The goal of the futures grid is to earn small profits from each price movement, whether the market is going up or down or staying within a range.

  1. Smart Arbitrage

OKX smart arbitrage helps traders make steady profits while reducing the risk of price changes in the market. It uses a Delta-neutral strategy, which means holding equal but opposite positions in two markets:

  • Buying a cryptocurrency in the spot market (long position).
  • Selling the same cryptocurrency in the perpetual swap market (short position).

This bot helps balance gains and losses, so price changes have less impact, and profits come from funding fees earned during the holding period. There are two types of smart arbitrage strategies on OKX:

  • Custom Mode: You choose your strategy and set profit targets.
  • Smart Mode: The system recommends the best strategy and automatically manages profit-taking, stop-loss, and adjustments.

Unlike smart arbitrage, there are four ways to set up the OKX futures and spot bots. You can either set the parameters based on your analysis, fill in parameters recommended by the crypto trading bot, use AI strategy, or copy lead traders’ winning bots.

OKX Copy Trading

OKX copy trading is a program that allows new users to copy strategies from more advanced traders and automatically execute them in the spot or futures markets. When you copy a seasoned trader, you will imitate their trades and automatically open and close positions when the trader you copy opens or closes theirs.

Transaction fees for the trades users copy are usually the same as the regular fees for the user’s tier level. However, you will need to share your profit with the lead trader, usually about 8 – 13% of your results. Additionally, you can set a maximum amount per order and a maximum amount for the trader you are copying.

For instance, you can set your maximum amount per order at 50 USDT and your maximum amount for the trader at 500 USDT.  After the lead trader has opened 10 positions, you will have an invested margin of 500 USDT, which is your maximum limit. So, if the trader opens an eleventh position, you won’t copy them.

OKX Wallet

OKX Wallet is now one of the best-decentralized wallets on the market. It supports many blockchain networks and enables users to access and explore the Web3 world. Unlike the OKXX exchange, with the OKX wallet, you have full control of your assets and private keys because the wallet is entirely decentralized and non-custodial.

The OKX Web3 wallet is designed to provide a full-fledged and seamless Web3 experience. It has a built-in DEX aggregator for multi-chain and cross-chain transactions, so you can switch between supported networks instead of creating multiple wallets on various chains.

Additionally, you can engage in yield farming, go through the NFT marketplace, and explore over 1,000 DApp protocols. Now, here are the benefits of using the OKX web3 wallet:

  • Gives you full control and ownership of your assets and wallet.
  • Quick crypto withdrawals without an approval process, unlike crypto exchanges.
  • Multi-chain wallet that automatically recognizes and connects to different blockchain technology networks without requiring manual user switching.
  • Manage crypto assets on over 60 chains, including Ethereum, Aptos, Optimism, and BSC.
  • Available on iOS, Android, and web browsers.

Remember that the OKX Web3 wallet does not save your seed phrase, private key, or password; you are responsible for these.

OKX Mobile App

OKX offers a mobile app with a user-friendly interface for buying, selling, trading, and managing crypto even when you are on the move. Unlike the desktop interface, the OKX app provides a simple and clean view, perfect for beginners, and an advanced mode for more experienced traders.

The OKX app is available on Apple Store and Play Store, and the registration process is straightforward. While the mobile app version is faster and more user-friendly, it still has all the tools available on the web interface and everything you need to manage your digital assets.

With a few taps, you can easily buy, sell, and convert crypto using fiat or other crypto assets, even though fiat withdrawals may not be as smooth as crypto withdrawals. Users can also explore the various trading options, set limits, and market orders with TP/SL, trail stops, etc., as you would do in the desktop version.

In addition, the OKX app offers margin trading with leverage of up to 10X. For derivatives, its futures contracts and perpetual swaps have leverage up to 125X, and you can set alerts to receive notifications when specific changes occur in your trades.

How to Open New Account and Trade on OKX?

Follow these steps to open an account and trade on OKX.

Step 1: Select your country or region and agree to the terms and privacy agreement, then click “Next.”

Step 2: Use your email to register and add the OKX referral code “CNJREVIEW.”

Step 3: OKX will email you a verification code. Once you add the code, it’s time to verify your number. They will send you another code via text.

Step 4: Create a secure password to protect your OKX account. We recommend creating at least a 12-word long password.

Step 5: Verify your identity by completing the KYC verification process. OKX will verify your documents within 24 hours.

To start trading crypto on OKX, follow the following steps:

Step 1: Deposit Funds

You need to fund your OKX account to begin cryptocurrency trading on OKX. You can deposit cryptocurrency from another wallet or use fiat options like credit cards (Visa, Mastercard), bank transfers, or peer-to-peer (P2P) transactions.

If you want to deposit crypto, go to the ‘Assets’ tab and select ‘Deposit.’ Choose the cryptocurrency and the network you want to deposit. Then, transfer the cryptocurrency to the generated wallet address.

Step 2: Choose Your Trading Method

Go to the ‘Trade’ section to see the various trading options OKX crypto exchange offers. Depending on the kind of trade you want to do, choose between spot or derivatives (futures, margin, and perpetual swaps).

For beginners, starting with the spot market or using the copy trading tool to imitate experienced traders is advisable.

Step 3: Place Your First Trade

Select the pair you want from the spot or futures market, like PEPE/USDT or BTC/USDT. Since this is your first trade, we recommend you use a small amount of money to trade.

Use the order window on the right to place buy or sell orders. You can choose between different order types:

  • Market Orders: Execute immediately at current prices.
  • Limit Orders: Set a specific price you want to buy or sell crypto.
  • Stop Orders: Execute when a certain price condition is met.

Finally, confirm your order, and it will be executed according to the order types you choose.

Does OKX Require KYC?

Yes, OKX does require KYC. The process is similar to that of other exchanges. To confirm your identity, you must submit personal identification documents, such as a selfie, a passport, or a driver’s license. Ensure that the information on your ID matches the region/country you picked during the account registration process.

Is OKX Safe and Legit to Trade Crypto and Bitcoin?

OKX is safe and legitimate to trade crypto and Bitcoin. The platform is considered as one of the best cryptocurrency exchanges with the cleanest interfaces. It is designed with simple and advanced modes to cater to various users. Additionally, if you are a beginner, the mobile app is better for learning, and you don’t have to worry about missing anything because it has all the features on the desktop version.

OKX offers some security features, including offline asset storage, a risk shield, multi-factor authentication, passkeys, anti-phishing codes, and withdrawal address whitelisting.

  1. Cold Wallet Storage

95% of assets on OKX are stored in offline wallets, which are not susceptible to hacks and security breaches. The company limits how much cryptocurrency can be stored in a single cold wallet address to further protect user funds assets stored offline.

Each address can hold a maximum of 1,000 BTC. This spreads the total amount of offline assets across multiple wallets, preventing a single point of failure. Once the funds in one cold wallet are withdrawn, new deposits will no longer be received.

  1. OKX Risk Shield

OKX crypto exchange sets aside a percentage of the platform’s assets, over $700 million, to safeguard money and users from potential breaches. The risk fund is similar to Binance’s Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), which protects against security breaches and market volatility.

3. Multi-factor Authentication

Once you open an account on OKX, it is important to up your security. You can do this through the profile icon. There, you will find various security measures to activate.

Start with two-factor authentication (2FA), then activate passkeys and authenticators. If you decide to activate the Google Authenticator app, keep the code you will be given safely. If you lose your phone or change devices, you can use it to log in to your authenticator app.

4. Anti-phishing Codes

This security feature allows users to double-proof their account security. When you activate it, OKX will email you a code that helps you differentiate between legitimate communications and suspicious emails.

5. Proof of Reserves

OKX published their December 2024 proof of reserve data and they’re holding over USD 30.8 billion in reserves. This includes some of the most popular cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin (105%), Ethereum (102%), and stablecoins such as Tether USDT (106%) and USD Coin (100%).

The PoR is published monthly, and the company uses advanced cryptographic methods, including zero-knowledge proofs, to ensure full transparency while protecting user privacy. You can independently verify your assets through OKX’s dashboard and public wallet addresses.

6. Withdrawal Address Whitelisting

OKX allows users to choose which wallet addresses are allowed for withdrawals through the address whitelisting feature. Any address outside the pre-approved addresses will automatically be blocked. So, even if someone tries to hack into your account, they cannot move funds to any address since they are not on the list.

title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO After Board’s Unanimous Vote
summary: Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as its president and chief executive officer following a unanimous board vote, reversing his sudden departure less than two weeks ago.
content:
Skip to content
Assets: NVDA

Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as its president and chief executive officer following a unanimous board vote, reversing his sudden departure less than two weeks ago.

The decision returns the company’s co-founder to its top leadership position amid ongoing investigations and heightened scrutiny over national security concerns.

In a November 23 announcement, Nvidia confirmed that Huang had also resumed his position as a member of the board, effective immediately. The decision followed several discussions and meetings between Huang and directors, who said they were satisfied with his candor and ability to lead the company.

The board also considered input from senior U.S. government officials before approving his return. According to Nvidia, that input gave directors confidence that reinstating Huang would not create a national security risk.

Nvidia Board Unanimously Approves Jensen Huang’s Return

Harvey C. Jones, Nvidia’s board chair, said directors believe Huang remains the right person to lead the company through its next phase of growth.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” Jones said in the announcement.

NVIDIA’s board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as president, CEO, and board director effective immediately, reversing a recent CEO transition. Source: @nvidianewsroom/X

The decision marks a significant reversal from the leadership changes announced earlier in November. On November 12, Nvidia disclosed that Huang had resigned as president, CEO, and board director, effective immediately. The board subsequently appointed longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO while beginning the process of identifying a permanent successor.

Huang’s departure followed reports involving personal relationships and concerns about a possible foreign intelligence operation. Media coverage also raised questions about potential national security implications involving individuals connected to China.

According to subsequent reporting by Reuters and The Associated Press, the circumstances surrounding his departure attracted attention from U.S. authorities and prompted broader scrutiny of the company’s leadership and compliance arrangements.

Huang’s reinstatement does not bring the internal investigation to an end. Nvidia confirmed that the independent committee established to examine reports of a foreign intelligence effort targeting its founder will continue its work until completion.

Foreign Intelligence Investigation Remains Open

Nvidia initially announced its independent investigation on November 8, following reports that Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.

The company appointed a committee consisting exclusively of independent directors and retained outside legal counsel to oversee the inquiry. The board said at the time that it had no reason to believe national security or Nvidia’s confidential information had been compromised, although it intended to examine all available information.

The November 23 announcement maintains that commitment. Nvidia said Huang supports the investigation and has agreed to cooperate fully until the process concludes.

The distinction is important: the board’s assessment that his return presents no national security risk does not mean the underlying investigation has been completed.

The company’s latest decision also follows public support for Huang’s return from prominent figures, including U.S. President Donald Trump. Brave New Coin reported that Trump had encouraged Nvidia to bring its founder back after the board initially indicated that reinstatement was not under consideration.

The president subsequently welcomed the reversal, describing it as the correct decision.

Nevertheless, questions surrounding the circumstances of Huang’s departure remain relevant to the company’s governance and regulatory responsibilities. Nvidia has also faced scrutiny over potential export-control and other compliance issues, according to media reports.

Nvidia Establishes New Compliance Oversight

Alongside Huang’s reinstatement, Nvidia is introducing additional governance measures intended to strengthen oversight of national security risks and international trade compliance.

The board has established a National Security and Export Control Committee, consisting entirely of independent directors. Its responsibilities include supervising trade compliance and assessing national security risks associated with the company’s operations.

NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has formed a dedicated committee to oversee national security and export control matters. Source: @nvidianewsroom/X

The committee is also engaging legal counsel with experience in national security matters. Those advisers will bring in additional specialists to support its work.

Nvidia is separately beginning a search for a Chief Compliance Officer. The new executive will oversee compliance across the company and report to the board’s Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee.

These measures indicate that Nvidia intends to maintain closer oversight of regulatory and security-related matters even as Huang returns to executive leadership.

Jones also acknowledged Kress’s contribution during the transition, thanking her for managing the company as interim CEO while continuing her responsibilities as chief financial officer.

Kress will now return to her previous executive responsibilities. She has served as the company’s CFO since September 2013 and has been responsible for overseeing its financial organization during a period of substantial expansion.

Jensen Huang Signals Renewed Commitment to Nvidia

In his statement following the reinstatement, Huang expressed appreciation for the board’s decision and acknowledged the responsibility of returning to lead the company.

“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” Huang said.

He also thanked Jones, Kress, Nvidia’s executive team, employees, shareholders, and business partners for their support during the leadership transition.

Jensen Huang updates his X bio and adds “CEO of Nvidia” to his title. Source: @JensenHuang/X

Huang described Nvidia as one of the world’s most consequential technology companies and said he was eager to resume his responsibilities.

His return restores the company’s familiar leadership structure at a time when demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure continues to shape the semiconductor industry.

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has overseen its transformation from a graphics processing unit manufacturer into a central supplier of computing hardware and software for artificial intelligence, data centers, and accelerated computing.

That history has made his leadership closely associated with the company’s corporate strategy and long-term direction. His unexpected departure therefore created uncertainty around the company’s succession planning and executive decision-making.

Nvidia Stock Rallies Following Leadership Reversal

Financial markets reacted positively to the reinstatement announcement. According to Reuters, Nvidia shares surged approximately 33% in early trading on November 23, as investors responded to the return of its long-serving founder.

The announcement also helped revive sentiment across technology and artificial intelligence stocks following recent weakness in the sector. Reuters reported gains in broader U.S. equity benchmarks, including the Nasdaq and S&P 500, during the session.

However, the immediate market reaction does not resolve the governance and regulatory questions surrounding Nvidia. Investors will continue monitoring the independent investigation, the company’s compliance initiatives, and any further developments involving U.S. authorities.

For now, Huang’s return restores continuity at the top of Nvidia while placing additional responsibility on its board to demonstrate that the company can maintain effective oversight.

The independent investigation will continue, and Nvidia has pledged to cooperate with government inquiries. The outcome of those processes, alongside the implementation of its new compliance framework, will remain important developments for the company in the coming weeks.
